scenario: A runaway trolley will kill five people unless you pull a lever, which redirects it onto a track where it will kill one person. You cannot stop it another way. Do you pull the lever?
actions: Pull the lever, redirecting the trolley toward one person
Do not pull the lever, allowing the trolley to continue toward five people
Shout urgent warnings to everyone on both tracks

source_testimonies.utilitarian:
Utilitarian assessment

1. Concrete consequences for directly-affected persons  
   • If you do nothing: the trolley kills the five people (certain, high-magnitude harm: five deaths). The lone person survives (one life saved).  
   • If you pull the lever: the trolley kills the one person (certain, high-magnitude harm: one death). The five survive (five lives saved).

2. Probability × magnitude comparison  
   Death is an irreversible, very large negative utility. With certainty (≈1.0 probability in the scenario), pulling the lever prevents four additional deaths. Saving four lives greatly outweighs the disutility of causing one death. As the corpus notes, “When the numbers become extreme, our intuitions must yield. If the alternative is a hundred thousand deaths, the wrongness of harming one innocent person becomes tragically outweighed.” The same logic applies at a smaller scale: preventing four extra deaths yields a large net benefit.

3. Rule-utilitarian or wider social effects  
   The scenario gives no evidence that this single, unseen act will be public, set a precedent, or undermine overall trust in rail-safety systems. Therefore speculative ripple effects should receive little weight relative to the certain life-and-death outcomes.

4. Missing information that could reverse the judgment  
   • If the lone person had extraordinarily high future welfare potential and each of the five were already terminally ill, the utility calculus could shift.  
   • If pulling the lever somehow created a broader practice that routinely sacrifices minorities, long-term social harm might outweigh the immediate benefit. No such facts are provided.  
   Because these possibilities are merely hypothetical and not supported by the description, they do not alter the expected outcome.

5. Conditional verdict  
   Given the stated facts—equal probability of death, no relevant differences in the victims’ future well-being, and no evidence of larger negative social repercussions—pulling the lever maximizes expected total well-being. As another corpus passage says, “If it is in our power to prevent something bad from happening, without thereby sacrificing anything of comparable moral importance, we ought, morally, to do it.” Sacrificing one life to save five averts a substantially greater harm; the sacrifice is not “of comparable moral importance” to the four additional deaths prevented.

Utilitarian recommendation: Pull the lever, unless further information shows that the lone person’s continued life would create far more well-being than that of the five combined or that the act would trigger significant negative systemic effects.
source_testimonies.deontological:
Maxim 1  
1. “Whenever I confront a runaway trolley heading toward five people, I will intentionally redirect it onto another track in order to save the five, even though this will kill the one person on that track.”  
2. Universal-law test: All rational agents could not will this maxim, because it requires every agent to make intentional lethal use of an innocent person as a mere means to an end. A world in which intentional killing of innocents is a standing rule undermines each person’s secure possession of life and thus contradicts the very capacity for rational willing.  
3. Duty: autonomy. Redirecting the trolley subjects the solitary person to lethal force without that person’s consent. This violates the innate right each person has to govern his or her own body and life.  
4. Result: The maxim fails; it is impermissible to adopt.

Maxim 2  
1. “Whenever I confront a runaway trolley heading toward five people and the only alternative is to redirect it so that it will certainly kill another innocent person, I will refrain from intervening.”  
2. Universal-law test: All rational agents can coherently will this maxim. No one is used as a means; the deaths that occur are effects of the trolley’s initial motion, not the agent’s intention. The principle preserves the right of each person not to be intentionally harmed by another.  
3. Duty: autonomy. By refusing to impose lethal force on anyone, the agent respects each person’s status as an end in him- or herself.  
4. Result: The maxim passes; it is permissible to adopt.

Deontological Answer: One must not pull the lever.
source_testimonies.virtue:
Central virtue conflict: Compassionate concern for each life vs. responsible courage to act for the wider common good.

Practical-wisdom judgment (phronesis): Emulating the steady-hearted hero who can bear tragic necessity—like Antigone honoring both kin and polis—we accept that flourishing sometimes requires choosing the lesser harm while grieving the loss.

Action: Pull the lever, while acknowledging the inherent tragedy, later honoring the lone victim and fostering communal reflection so that such dilemmas arise less often.
source_testimonies.care:
I begin by noticing what the classic trolley vignette leaves out: Who are these six people?  What ties, histories, and dependencies weave them into the lives of others—and into mine?  Care ethics lives in those particulars.  In an actual emergency I would be scrambling to gather them:  Can I see faces, read name-tags, call out warnings, wave my arms, hit a brake, throw a rock into the gears, or in any other way keep everyone alive?  That impulse—to search creatively for a response that protects every vulnerable body—is the heart of care.

But the story insists that time has vanished and only one binary lever remains.  Stripped of further context, I must still stay in relationship to the people before me.  Five terrified persons will die if I stand inert; one terrified person will die if I act.  Nothing about the single person suggests deeper obligations to me than the five, nor do I know of special claims the five have that override the one.  Given that radical symmetry, the caring response is to move toward the greater need: five lives are poised to be lost and with them the networks of children, parents, friends, and coworkers who rely on them.  Honoring vulnerability and interdependence, I would pull the lever.

Doing so is not a triumph.  It is, at best, a tragic care: I reach out to five while letting another fall from my grasp.  Afterward, the residue of sorrow, responsibility, and perhaps guilt must not be brushed away as “the right calculation.”  I would feel obligated to:

• stay with the injured or dying person if possible, acknowledging their humanity rather than treating them as a mere statistic;  
• notify their loved ones, speak truthfully about what happened, and share their final words if any;  
• support grief counseling and material assistance for those who depended on them;  
• attend to my own moral distress, so that it does not curdle into numbness and diminish my capacity to care in the future.

Finally, I remember the warning from the corpus: “One cannot care for everyone; to try is to be overwhelmed and to lose the ethic of care itself.”  This dilemma thrusts that limit upon me.  Accepting the limit is painful, but refusing to decide—allowing five avoidable deaths—would be, in this narrow scenario, a greater abandonment of care.

So, with tears and moral attention rather than clean certainty, I would pull the lever—and then remain to tend the wounds, visible and invisible, that follow.

source_testimonies.rawlsian:
Rawlsian Ethics Answer

1. The relevant basic right  
   Behind the veil of ignorance no one would gamble with the most fundamental liberty—the right to life. Each person, no matter how “useful” to others, possesses “an inviolability founded on justice that even the welfare of society as a whole cannot override.” The single individual on the side-track enjoys the very same basic right to life as the five on the main track.

2. The prohibition on sacrificing one for the many  
   A policy or rule that licenses intentionally redirecting lethal force onto an innocent person treats that person as a means to others’ welfare. Such a rule conflicts with the first principle of justice, which protects equal basic liberties for all. Under Rawls’s framework we must reject “utilitarian trade-offs that violate individual liberties.”

3. Reasoning from the original position  
   • Imagine you do not know whether you will be the one person or one of the five.  
   • You must choose a general principle for such cases.  
   • Because you might occupy the position of the lone victim, rational prudence under the veil of ignorance leads you to forbid others from redirecting fatal threats onto you.  
   • This yields a rule: “No one may intentionally impose a lethal harm on an innocent third party, even to reduce the number of deaths.”  
   The parties reach reflective equilibrium on this rule because it preserves equal inviolability for every citizen.

4. The standpoint of the least advantaged  
   In this scenario the “least advantaged” is the isolated person who faces certain death if the lever is pulled. The difference principle instructs us to choose the option that does not worsen the position of the least advantaged relative to some feasible alternative. Pulling the lever eliminates that person’s very existence; refraining preserves the possibility—however slim—that the five might escape or be rescued, whereas the redirected track guarantees the lone individual’s death. Justice therefore sides with protecting the basic right of the most vulnerable party rather than counting lives.

5. Conclusion: Do not pull the lever  
   Acting would intentionally violate an innocent person’s equal right to life, a liberty that justice declares inviolable. Although the outcome is tragic either way, a Rawlsian agent must refuse to pull the lever, thereby upholding the principled priority of equal basic rights over aggregate welfare.
